definition: The Präsens is the German present tense, used for things happening now, habitually, or (unlike English) even for the near future: "Ich lerne Deutsch" can mean "I learn/am learning German" or "I'm going to learn German." Regular (weak) verbs drop -en from the infinitive and add person endings (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en); seven high-frequency strong verbs additionally change their stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms only, e.g. sehen → du siehst, er sieht.

German has nine personal pronoun forms because formal "you" (Sie) is grammatically distinct from informal du/ihr, and "she" and "they" share the identical form sie (only context or the verb ending distinguishes them: sie kommt = she comes, sie kommen = they come). Sie meaning "you" (formal) is always capitalized, in every position in the sentence, which is how a reader tells it apart from sie meaning "she"/"they."

German marks every noun's gender with an article: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter), die (plural) for "the"; ein, eine, ein for "a/an" (with no plural — Kinder, not "ein Kinder"). The article, not the noun's ending, is usually the only overt signal of gender, which is why gender is learned per noun, e.g. der Mann, die Frau, das Kind.

The nominative case marks the subject of the sentence — whoever or whatever performs the action — and is the form found by asking wer? (who?) or was? (what?): Wer spielt? → Der Mann spielt. It is the citation form of the article and the case a noun takes with no other case assigned to it, e.g. der Mann, die Frau, das Kind.

The accusative case marks the direct object of a transitive verb — the thing directly acted upon — found by asking wen? (whom?) or was? (what?): Ich sehe wen? → Ich sehe den Mann. Only the masculine article changes from the nominative (der→den, ein→einen); feminine, neuter and plural articles are identical in nominative and accusative.

In every German main clause the conjugated verb sits in position 2, no matter what occupies position 1. If something other than the subject — a time phrase, an adverb — takes position 1, the subject does not move to position 1 as in English; it moves to position 3, right after the verb: Heute lerne ich Deutsch (lit. "Today learn I German"), not *Heute ich lerne Deutsch. This subject-verb swap is called inversion, and it is a direct, mechanical consequence of V2, not a separate rule.

W-questions (wer, was, wo, wann, warum, wie, woher, wohin) put the question word in position 1 and the verb in position 2, so V2 word order is preserved: Wo wohnst du? Yes/no questions instead move the verb itself to position 1 with no question word: Wohnst du in Berlin?

German splits negation between two words depending on what is negated. kein negates a noun that would otherwise carry ein/eine or no article at all (Ich habe ein Buch → Ich habe kein Buch; Er trinkt Milch → Er trinkt keine Milch); nicht negates everything else — verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and nouns that already have der/die/das (Das Buch ist nicht gut). kein declines exactly like ein plus a plural, so keine also negates plural nouns that have no singular indefinite article.

es gibt (literally "it gives") is the fixed idiom for "there is/are," and it always takes an accusative object regardless of number: Es gibt einen Park hier (There is a park here); Es gibt viele Bäume (There are many trees) — gibt never agrees with the following noun, only with the invariant subject es. It is one of several fixed uses of impersonal es, alongside weather expressions like Es regnet and set phrases like Es tut mir leid.

The dative case marks the indirect object — the person who receives or benefits from the direct object — found by asking wem? (to/for whom?): Ich gebe dem Kind ein Buch. A handful of verbs (helfen, antworten, gefallen) take ONLY a dative object with no accusative at all, which trips up learners expecting a direct object. Dative plural nouns add -n unless they already end in -n or -s: die Kinder → den Kindern, but die Frauen → den Frauen.

Possessive articles (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr) decline exactly like ein across all cases — mein, meinen, meinem — so once a learner knows the ein-endings, the possessives are the same table with a different stem. euer is the one irregular: it drops its own -e- before any ending (euer → eure, euren, eurem), to avoid the awkward *eueren.

Der-words (dieser "this," jeder "every/each," welcher "which") decline exactly like the definite article der/die/das rather than like ein — so dieser mirrors der, diese mirrors die, and so on through all three cases (dieser Mann, diesen Mann, diesem Mann). jeder has no plural form, since "every" is inherently singular.

aliases: können wollen müssen sollen dürfen mögen
definition: The six modal verbs (können, wollen, müssen, sollen, dürfen, mögen, plus the subjunctive-derived möchten) all change their stem vowel in the singular (ich/du/er) while keeping the infinitive vowel in the plural, and ich and er/sie/es are always identical: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können. A modal occupies the normal V2 verb slot while the main verb it governs is pushed to the very end of the clause as a bare infinitive: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.
sequence: Conjugate the modal for the subject (ich kann)
Push the full main verb to the end as a bare infinitive

definition: The Perfekt is the everyday past tense of spoken German, built from a conjugated auxiliary (haben or sein) in V2 plus the Partizip II at the very end of the clause: Ich habe Fußball gespielt; Er ist nach Berlin gefahren. Unlike English, choice of auxiliary is not free — it is fixed per verb, mainly by whether the verb expresses movement/change of state (sein) or not (haben).
sequence: Pick haben or sein based on the verb
Conjugate that auxiliary for the subject and place it in V2
Form the Partizip II of the main verb and place it at the end

definition: The Partizip II is the past-participle form used inside the Perfekt and Plusquamperfekt. Weak (regular) verbs form it as ge- + stem + -t (spielen → gespielt); strong (irregular) verbs form it as ge- + stem, often with a vowel change, + -en (sehen → gesehen), and must simply be memorized. Two groups drop the ge- entirely: verbs ending in -ieren (studieren → studiert) and verbs with an inseparable prefix be-/emp-/ent-/er-/ge-/miss-/ver-/zer- (verstehen → verstanden).

aliases: an auf hinter in neben über unter vor zwischen
definition: Nine prepositions (an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen) take either the accusative or the dative depending on meaning, not on the preposition itself: dative answers wo? (location — already there), accusative answers wohin? (direction — moving there). Compare Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch (dative, static) with Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch (accusative, movement onto).

When an attributive adjective follows a der-word (der, die, das, dieser, jeder, welcher), the article already signals gender and case, so the adjective needs only a minimal "weak" ending: -e almost everywhere, and -en for accusative masculine and every plural, e.g. der große Mann (nom.) but den großen Mann (acc.). The underlying logic — one case signal per noun phrase — is what the corpus calls the Signal Rule.

When an attributive adjective has no article in front of it at all, it must carry the gender/case signal itself, so it takes a "strong" ending that mirrors the definite article's own endings: -er (like der), -e (like die), -es (like das), -en (like den), e.g. kalter Kaffee (nom. masc.) but kalten Kaffee (acc. masc.). This is the same Signal Rule as the weak endings, applied when no article is present to do the signaling.

dass (double s) is the subordinating conjunction "that," introducing a clause and pushing its verb to the end: Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt. das (single s) is the neuter definite article or demonstrative pronoun "the/that/it," which never sends a verb to the end: Das Buch ist gut. The two are spelled and pronounced identically apart from that one consonant, and confusing them is one of the most common native-writer as well as learner errors.

Adjective endings signal which declension applies: ein-words and der-words trigger weak or mixed endings, while a bare adjective before a noun takes strong endings that show case and gender themselves.
Some German adjectives govern a fixed preposition and case — stolz auf (+ accusative), zufrieden mit (+ dative). The combination is learned as one unit, exactly like verbs with prepositions.
Both mean 'when' in the past-versus-present split: als for a single completed past event (als ich Kind war), wenn for repeated past or any present/future events (wenn es regnet).
An apposition renames a noun in the same case right beside it: Herr Müller, der Direktor, kommt. It takes its case from the noun it explains, never from position.
The comparative (Komparativ) raises an adjective one degree — schnell → schneller — usually with an umlaut where the vowel allows it (groß → größer), and governs als for comparisons.

Irreal past conditions use hätte/wäre + past participle in the if-clause and würde + haben/sein + participle (or hätte/wäre + participle) in the main clause: Wenn ich gelernt hätte, hätte ich bestanden.
Sentence adverbs like trotzdem, deshalb and sonst occupy position one and force the finite verb into position two — inversion applies exactly as after any fronted element.
Prepositions fuse with da(r)- and wo(r)- to refer back or ask about things (not people): damit, davon, worauf. The -r- appears before vowels: darauf, worüber.

term: Dass Clause Vs Zu Infinitiv Choice
definition: Use zu + infinitive when the subordinate subject matches the main subject (Er hofft zu gewinnen); use a dass-clause when the subjects differ (Er hofft, dass sie gewinnt).
A closed group of verbs — helfen, danken, folgen, gefallen, gehören, antworten — governs the dative object where English uses a direct object. They never take an accusative object.
Connectors like allerdings, hingegen and nämlich organise argument across sentences. Each has a fixed position behaviour (some invert, some do not) that must be learned per word.
In a subordinate clause the Ersatzinfinitiv fronts the conjugated auxiliary before the cluster (Oberfeldumstellung): …, weil er hat kommen müssen — never *kommen müssen hat.

With modals in the perfect (and a few other verbs), German uses two infinitives instead of a participle: Er hat kommen müssen, not *gekonnt. The modal stays infinitive whenever a second infinitive is present.

Participles with their complements stand before the noun they modify, framed by commas in writing: die gestern Abend im Restaurant servierte Suppe. Everything between article and noun belongs to the attribute.
Futur I (werden + infinitive) expresses future time, but more often assumption or promise about the present: Er wird jetzt arbeiten — he is probably working now.
Futur II (werden + participle + haben/sein) expresses a completed future event or, more commonly, a conjecture about the past: Sie wird es vergessen haben.

The genitive marks possession and a small set of prepositions and verbs (wegen, während, trotz; sich schämen). In speech it is retreating before von + dative, but writing and formal registers keep it.
A closed set — wegen, während, trotz, statt, innerhalb, außerhalb — governs the genitive (wegen des Wetters). Colloquially they often appear with dative, which the standard still marks wrong.
Commands address du, ihr or Sie directly: Komm! Kommt! Kommen Sie! The du-form drops the -st (and usually the umlaut change stays: Nimm!), the Sie-form inverts with the pronoun kept.
Words like man, jemand, niemand, etwas, alles and jeder quantify without pointing: man generalises the subject, jemand/niemand assert or deny existence, etwas/alles grade quantity.
An indem-clause expresses means or simultaneity — indem er sparte (by saving), dadurch dass. Unlike um–zu it allows a different subject from the main clause.
Reported questions keep verb-final order and use ob for yes/no questions: Er fragt, ob du kommst. W-questions keep their question word: Sie fragt, wann der Zug fährt.
Reported speech shifts tenses back and, in formal writing, into Konjunktiv I: Er sagt, er sei krank. Colloquially the indicative with dass dominates.
Prefixes be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver- and zer- never separate and never take ge- in the participle: verstehen → verstanden. Stress falls on the stem, not the prefix.
Present/future unreal conditions use Konjunktiv II (or würde + infinitive) in both clauses: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, käme ich — or …würde ich kommen.
Proportional comparison pairs je + comparative with desto/umso + comparative, both clauses inverted: Je mehr du übst, desto besser wirst du.
Konjunktiv I marks reported speech in formal writing, built from the infinitive stem (er habe, sie werde). Only sein is visibly distinct everywhere, which is why the press loves it.
Where Konjunktiv I matches the indicative (wir haben, sie sagen), formal writing substitutes Konjunktiv II or würde-forms to keep the report visibly reported: Sie sagten, sie hätten Zeit.

Konjunktiv II marks unreality — wishes, hypotheticals, polite requests — built from the Präteritum stem with umlaut where possible (hätte, wäre, könnte). Where no distinct form exists, würde + infinitive steps in.
Past unreality uses hätte/wäre + past participle: Wenn ich das gewusst hätte… There is no würde-passive of the past to hide behind — the participle is obligatory.
German often avoids the passive with man + active verb: Man spricht hier Deutsch. It keeps the agent vague without any passive morphology.

After ein-words (ein, kein, mein…), adjectives take weak endings except in the three slots where the article itself shows no ending — nominative masculine -er (ein guter Mann), nominative and accusative neuter -es (ein gutes Kind).

Weak masculine nouns (Student, Kollege, Junge…) take -(e)n in every case except nominative singular: den Studenten, dem Kollegen. The Name-type adds -ns in the genitive instead (des Namens). Exception: das Herz is neuter — des Herzens, dem Herzen, die Herzen.
Partizip I (stem + -d: lachend) works as an adjective for ongoing action: das lachende Kind. Extended with complements it builds the participial constructions of formal style.
Partizip II works as an adjective for completed or passive states: die geschlossene Tür, ein erfahrener Arzt. It declines like any adjective and extends the same way.
The passive agent takes von for the doer (von der Polizei), durch for the means or intermediary (durch einen Boten), mit for the instrument (mit einem Messer).
The passive participle of werden is worden (not geworden) whenever a main-verb participle is present: Es ist gestohlen worden.
Modals combine with the passive infinitive (…muss repariert werden) and, in the perfect, trigger the double infinitive: Es hat repariert werden müssen.
The past perfect (hatte/war + participle) marks the earlier of two past events: Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er. Rare in speech, standard in narrative.
The simple past (ich machte, ich war, ich hatte) carries written narrative; speech prefers Perfekt except for sein, haben and modals, which stay in Präteritum even when spoken.
Reflexive pronouns stand in the accusative unless the verb already has an accusative object or the body part is involved — then dative: Ich wasche mich vs Ich wasche mir die Hände.
Reflexive verbs (sich erinnern, sich freuen) require the reflexive pronoun as a fixed partner; the dictionary marks whether it stands in accusative or dative.
Relative clauses follow their noun with verb-final order, opened by der/die/das-forms matching the noun's gender and number and the clause's case: der Mann, den ich sah.
After indefinite or whole-clause antecedents German uses was (Alles, was…), wo for places, and wer/wen/wem for people without a named antecedent: Wer zuerst kommt….
sein + zu + infinitive expresses possibility or necessity passively: Das ist zu machen (can/must be done). The subject is the thing acted upon.
Separable prefixes (ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, vor-, zu-…) jump to clause end in main clauses (Ich stehe auf) and rejoin with ge- between prefix and stem in the participle (aufgestanden).
sich lassen + infinitive expresses possibility like können: Das lässt sich machen (that can be done). The subject is the patient, the agent unmentioned.
The superlative (schnellste, höchste) takes -st with umlaut where possible, and predicatively uses am …-sten: am schnellsten. Irregular: gut → best, viel → meist.

Strong and irregular verbs form Konjunktiv II synthetically from the Präteritum stem with umlaut (käme, nähme, wüsste); weak verbs fall back to würde + infinitive because their forms match the indicative.
A tiny group — lehren, nennen, schimpfen — takes two accusative objects in older grammar (Er lehrt mich Deutsch); modern style usually rephrases one as a prepositional phrase.
Purpose with the same subject in both clauses uses um + zu + infinitive at the clause end: Er lernt, um zu bestehen. Different subjects need damit instead.
Intransitive verbs form a subjectless passive with es: Es wird getanzt. The es vanishes on inversion (Hier wird getanzt), but the verb stays singular.
Valency is the case frame a verb governs — zustimmen takes dative, warten takes auf + accusative. The dictionary marks it (+D, +A) because no rule predicts it.
Many verbs bind a fixed preposition + case: warten auf (+A), sich freuen über (+A), leiden unter (+D). Preposition and case are memorised with the verb as one unit.
The process passive (werden + participle) describes what is being done: Das Haus wird gebaut. Werden conjugates for tense and mood; the participle never changes.
Both mean 'because' with verb-final order; da fronts known or framing reasons (Da es regnet, bleiben wir), weil delivers the new information, usually after the main clause.
Werden builds the future (wird kommen), the passive (wird gebaut) and, as a full verb, means 'become' (wird Arzt). One form, three jobs — the paradigm tables keep them apart.
Würde + infinitive is the analytic Konjunktiv II, used wherever no distinct synthetic form exists (weak verbs) and colloquially almost everywhere: Ich würde kommen.
Dependent infinitives take zu before the verb (separable verbs tuck it between prefix and stem: anzufangen), governed by verbs, adjectives and nouns that require it: versuchen zu kommen.
The statal passive (sein + participle) describes the state after the action: Die Tür ist geschlossen. Contrast werden-passive (process) vs sein-passive (result).
Paired conjunctions frame two clauses or phrases: entweder…oder, weder…noch, sowohl…als auch, zwar…aber. Word order follows the conjunction each half starts with.
